description: We are Team Astro_Verse; Juthy, Naziya, Chandon, and Tuhin innovating together for sustainable agriculture. Our primary challenge is enabling cultivation under extreme water conditions. Currently, our solution addresses this water crisis while also providing farmers with real-time weather alerts. In the future, we plan to tackle soil toxicity, focusing on detecting microplastics in soil. Additionally, we aim to build an app that shows the market demand and price of any crop before cultivation.
summary: Astrapon is a web app that helps a farmer compare crop rotations for their own field before planting. The farmer draws the field on a map and records what they grew. Astrapon then brings in NASA weather, NASA satellite rain and soil data for that exact place, replays the farmer's current rotation and better-fitting alternatives through 20 years of real past weather, and ranks them by what matters to the farmer: water, soil cover, crop diversity and weather risk. A 3D replay, a plain-language "Why this option?" view and a spoken summary in English or Bangla explain the trade-offs. A Water & Energy planner shows nearby water, when ponds may run low, and the pump and solar size for the dry season.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Astrapon is a web app that lets a farmer test a new crop rotation on their own field before risking a season. The farmer finds their field by place name, coordinates or device location, draws its boundary on a satellite map, and records what they grew, when they planted and harvested, their soil tests, water limits and what matters most to them.

A background worker then brings in data for that exact place: NASA POWER daily weather since 1981, NASA GPM IMERG daily satellite rain for the field's 11 km cell since 1998, and soil water capacity from ISRIC SoilGrids (or USDA SSURGO in the US). NASA SMAP soil moisture and MODIS greenness are optional. Every value is checked for units, dates and missing days and stored with its source, version and a checksum.

Astrapon rebuilds the farmer's current rotation from their history and searches for alternatives that respect their limits, local planting windows and rotation rules. Our simulation engine replays every option day by day through the same 20 years of real weather using the FAO-56 water balance: crop water use, rain, runoff, soil water, crop stress, irrigation need, and frost and heat exposure. The options are ranked by the farmer's own priorities and tested against dry starts and the driest and wettest years.

Results come as an "at a glance" card, a 3D replay of the seasons, a comparison table, a plain-language "Why this option?" view and a spoken summary in English or Bangla. A Water & Energy planner shows nearby rivers and ponds, groundwater depth from monitoring wells, the months when ponds may run low, the regional water trend from NASA GRACE, and the pump and solar panel size for the dry season.

What benefits does it have?

- Farmers see how each option would have done in real past seasons on their own field, without risking a harvest.

- Trade-offs are clear: water saved, bare soil, crop variety and weather risk, each marked better or worse than what they grow now.

- Dry-season water and solar pump planning in the same place as the crop decision.

- Every number shows its source and resolution. Missing data stays missing and is never guessed.

- The same inputs always give the same result, so a plan can be checked, shared and exported.

What is the intended impact?

We want smallholder farmers and extension workers, starting in Bangladesh, to make climate-aware rotation decisions backed by NASA data instead of guesswork. That means using less irrigation water, keeping soils covered and diverse, and being ready before the dry season. The Bangla interface and voice let farmers use satellite data without reading charts. The app works for fields anywhere in the world. Astrapon supports the farmer's judgment: it does not forecast yield, profit or future weather, and it tells the farmer to check results with a local adviser.

What tools, languages, hardware and software did we use?

- Languages: TypeScript, SQL

- Frontend: Next.js 16, React 19, Material UI, MapLibre GL, three.js with React Three Fiber for the 3D replay

- Backend and data: Supabase (PostgreSQL, PostGIS, row-level security, authentication), a Node.js background worker on GitHub Actions, zod for data validation

- Testing: Vitest (348 automated tests), Playwright for browser checks

- Hosting: Vercel

- Data: NASA POWER, GPM IMERG (through NASA Earthdata Harmony), SMAP, MODIS, GRACE/GRACE-FO, NASA GIBS, ISRIC SoilGrids, USDA SSURGO, OpenStreetMap, FAO-56 and the FAO Crop Calendar

- AI in the app: OpenAI text-to-speech for the Bangla and English voice summary. We also used an AI coding assistant during development.

- Hardware: standard laptops only. No special hardware is needed, and the app runs in any modern browser.

How is our project creative?

Most farm tools show weather maps or give one recommendation without explaining it. Astrapon turns NASA data into a "what if" for one farmer's field: it replays the farmer's real rotation and the alternatives side by side on the same past seasons, and shows it in 3D on the farmer's own field shape. Every result explains itself, from why an option ranks where it does to which data it used and what is still unknown. We connect the crop decision to water and energy, so a farmer sees both the rotation and the solar pump it would need. Satellite results are spoken in Bangla, so farmers can use them without reading a chart.

What factors did our team consider?

- Honesty: separate evidence types (satellite, model, survey, farmer report). Never invent or blend data, never present scores as probabilities, and state the limits.

- Local fit: use the farmer's own dates and planting windows. Never impose one country's seasons on another. Use crop values measured in South Asia where FAO-56 has none, such as jute from a Bangladeshi study.

- Accessibility: Bangla and English, voice, simple language, works on low-end devices with a 3D quality setting and a reduced-motion option.

- Data quality: the resolution of every source, missing days, the Final vs Late Run of IMERG (gauge calibration matters), and the time-zone difference between datasets.

- Privacy and security: each farmer's data is private by database row-level security, and secrets stay on the server.

- Reproducibility: a versioned engine, pinned data and checksums, so any result can be re-run exactly.

- Limits we acknowledge: past weather is not a forecast, grid cells are coarser than fields, and the tool has not yet been validated in field trials.
